title: Particle Physics and Recent Trends

toc.title: 22.1 Particles and antiparticles; leptons and quarks; the Higgs boson
22.3 The Big Bang theory and Hubble's law

html:
The last chapter of the Physics paper looks outward twice: inward to the smallest objects we know, and outward to the whole universe. Modern Physics carries 12 of the 50 Physics questions (official MEC weightage), and we estimate about 2 come from here. The paper asks for the inventory — six quarks, six leptons, which particles make a proton, which force is carried by which boson — and for the evidence behind the Big Bang, especially Hubble's law. Nothing needs a long calculation; what it needs is precision, because this is the area where careless books print sentences that are simply false.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Six quarks (u, d, c, s, t, b) with charges +\frac{2}{3} and -\frac{1}{3}; six leptons (e, μ, τ and their neutrinos); antiparticles for every particle.
  • Hadrons: baryons are three quarks (p = uud, n = udd), mesons are a quark–antiquark pair (\pi^+=u\bar d).
  • The four interactions, their exchange bosons, ranges and approximate relative strengths.
  • The Higgs boson: quantum of the Higgs field, about 125 GeV/c^2, found at CERN in 2012; it gives mass to fundamental particles, not to everything.
  • Nanotechnology: the 1–100 nm scale, why the properties change, and two or three real applications.
  • The Big Bang: expansion, the CMB at 2.7 K, redshift, v=H_0d, and the age estimate 1/H_0\approx14 Gyr (accepted age 13.8 Gyr).

22.1 Particles and antiparticles; leptons and quarks; the Higgs boson

22.1.1 The inventory

By the 1970s the hundreds of particles found in cosmic rays and accelerators had been reduced to a small list of fundamental particles — particles with no known internal structure. This list is the Standard Model.

Family Members Charge Notes
Quarks (6) up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom +\frac{2}{3} (u, c, t); -\frac{1}{3} (d, s, b) feel the strong force; never found alone
Leptons (6) electron, muon, tau -1 feel the weak force and, if charged, electromagnetism
electron neutrino, muon neutrino, tau neutrino 0 almost massless; feel only the weak force
Gauge bosons photon, gluon, W^+, W^-, Z^0 0, 0, ±1, 0 carry the forces
Higgs boson H^0 0 gives mass to the fundamental particles

The quarks and leptons come in three generations of increasing mass: (u, d, e, \nu_e), then (c, s, μ, \nu_\mu), then (t, b, τ, \nu_\tau). Ordinary matter uses only the first generation plus the muon and neutrinos made in cosmic-ray showers and radioactive decays.

22.1.2 Antiparticles

For every particle there is an antiparticle with the same mass and opposite charge (and opposite quantum numbers). The antiparticle of the electron is the positron (e^+); of the proton, the antiproton; of the neutrino, the antineutrino; of a quark, the antiquark.

Two processes matter for the paper:

  • Annihilation. A particle and its antiparticle can disappear, their mass-energy appearing as radiation. An electron and a positron at rest give two photons, each of energy m_ec^2=0.511 MeV, travelling in opposite directions so that momentum is conserved. Two photons, not one: a single photon could not carry away zero momentum.
  • Pair production. A photon of sufficient energy near a nucleus can create an electron–positron pair. The minimum energy is 2m_ec^2=1.02 MeV, and any excess becomes kinetic energy of the pair. A single photon in empty space cannot do this — momentum conservation again requires a third body, the nucleus.
Worked example 22.1 — the photons from an annihilation

Problem. An electron and a positron, both nearly at rest, annihilate. Find the energy of each photon in joules and the wavelength of the radiation.

Solution. The total rest energy is 2m_ec^2=1.02 MeV, shared equally, so each photon has 0.511 MeV =0.511\times10^{6}\times1.6\times10^{-19}=8.2\times10^{-14} J.

\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{E}=\dfrac{1.99\times10^{-25}}{8.2\times10^{-14}} =2.4\times10^{-12} m =2.4 pm.

Check. 2.4 pm is a gamma ray, far shorter than any X-ray tube produces. The two photons must also travel in opposite directions, so that the total momentum stays zero.

Antimatter is not "negative mass"

An antiparticle has positive mass and positive energy. Only its charge and its other quantum numbers are reversed. Antimatter does not fall upwards, and it does not have negative energy. It annihilates with matter because particle number is not conserved in that interaction, not because the masses cancel.

22.1.3 Quarks and hadrons

Quarks are never found in isolation. They are held by the strong force, whose carrier is the gluon, and the force grows as quarks are pulled apart: separating two quarks creates a new quark–antiquark pair rather than a free quark. This is confinement, and it is why every experiment sees only combinations of quarks.

Combination Name Examples
three quarks (qqq) baryon proton uud, neutron udd, \Lambda (uds), \Omega^- (sss)
quark + antiquark (q\bar q) meson \pi^+=u\bar d, \pi^-=\bar ud, K^+=u\bar s

Both classes are hadrons — particles that feel the strong force. The charges work out exactly:

p=uud:\ \tfrac{2}{3}+\tfrac{2}{3}-\tfrac{1}{3}=+1, \qquad n=udd:\ \tfrac{2}{3}-\tfrac{1}{3}-\tfrac{1}{3}=0

\pi^+=u\bar d:\ \tfrac{2}{3}-\left(-\tfrac{1}{3}\right)=+1

Notice that the neutron is neutral even though all three of its quarks are charged: the charges simply add to zero. That is a favourite exam trap.

Baryon number is a conserved quantity: each quark has B=+\frac{1}{3}, each antiquark -\frac{1}{3}. A proton or neutron therefore has B=+1, a meson has B=0, and in any reaction the total baryon number is unchanged. This is why the proton cannot decay into a positron and a pion, for example: those have B=0, and B must be conserved. No proton decay has ever been observed (the experimental limit on its lifetime is beyond 10^{34} years).

22.1.4 The four fundamental interactions

Interaction Exchange boson Range Relative strength Acts on
Strong gluon (8 kinds) about 10^{-15} m (a nucleon) 1 quarks and therefore hadrons
Electromagnetic photon infinite (1/r^2) about 10^{-2} all charged particles
Weak W^+, W^-, Z^0 about 10^{-18} m about 10^{-6} all quarks and leptons
Gravitational graviton (not yet observed) infinite about 10^{-38} everything with mass-energy

The numbers in the strength column are approximate and depend on which pair of particles is being compared; they are meant only to rank the forces. Two protons in a nucleus repel each other electrically and are held together by the strong force, which is about a hundred times stronger at nuclear distances. Gravity, weaker than the strong force by some 38 powers of ten, only becomes important when a very large mass is collected together — which is why it rules the planets and the galaxies but not the nucleus.

The weak interaction is the one responsible for beta decay: a neutron turns into a proton by emitting a W^-, which becomes an electron and an antineutrino. It is weak in strength but essential — without it the Sun could not burn hydrogen by the proton–proton chain.

Generations and carriers

Quarks: up down, charm strange, top bottom — "up down, charm strange, top bottom" in pairs. Leptons: the three charged ones (e, μ, τ) and their three neutrinos. Bosons: gluon for glue (strong), photon for electromagnetism, W/Z for the weak force, and the Higgs on its own.

22.1.5 The Higgs boson

Most of the Standard Model works with massless particles. But the W and Z bosons are heavy (80.4 and 91.2 GeV/c^2), and quarks and leptons have mass. The Higgs mechanism explains this: the universe is filled with a field — the Higgs field — and particles that interact with it behave as if they have mass. The Higgs boson is the quantum of that field, the ripple that can be produced in a collision.

The Higgs boson was discovered at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012, with a mass of about 125 GeV/c^2 — about 133 times the mass of a proton. Higgs and Englert shared the 2013 Nobel Prize for the theory.

What the Higgs does and does not do

It gives mass to fundamental particles — the W and Z bosons, the quarks and the charged leptons — through their interaction with the field. It does not give mass to the photon or the gluon (they remain massless), and it is not the source of most of the mass of a proton or a neutron. About 99 % of a nucleon's mass is the energy of the gluon field and of the confined quarks, converted by E=mc^2. Saying "the Higgs gives mass to everything" is wrong, and it is exactly the sort of sentence a sloppy book prints.

One more honest qualification: in the original Standard Model the neutrinos are massless, but neutrino oscillation (one flavour turning into another) shows that they have small, different masses. That is a known gap between the simplest version of the model and experiment, and it is why neutrino physics is an active field.

22.2 Nanotechnology

22.2.1 The scale

A nanometre is 10^{-9} m — one millionth of a millimetre. Nanotechnology is the design and use of structures with at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 100 nm. For comparison:

Object Size
hydrogen atom about 0.1 nm
width of a DNA double helix about 2 nm
a typical protein 5–10 nm
a small virus 20–300 nm
gate length in a modern processor a few nm
red blood cell about 7 000 nm (7 μm)
human hair about 80 000 nm (80 μm)

22.2.2 Why the properties change

Two things happen when a piece of material is made very small.

  1. Surface dominates. The fraction of atoms on the surface grows as 1/r. A 10 nm particle has roughly a fifth of its atoms on the surface, so surface chemistry — catalysis, adhesion, dissolution — controls its behaviour.
  2. Quantum effects appear. When the particle is smaller than the electron's quantum wavelength, the allowed energies become discrete, and the colour, melting point and electrical behaviour change with size. Gold nanoparticles, for example, are red or purple rather than golden, and their colour depends on their diameter.

22.2.3 Real applications

  • Medicine — targeted drug delivery. Drugs are packaged in liposomes or polymer nanoparticles of 50–200 nm, which can pass through leaky tumour blood vessels and release the drug where it is needed, reducing side effects. Several such formulations are in clinical use.
  • Water treatment. Nanoscale iron particles and nanomembranes remove arsenic and other contaminants from groundwater. This matters in the Terai, where arsenic in tube-well water is a real public-health problem.
  • Materials and coatings. Titanium dioxide and zinc oxide nanoparticles make transparent sunscreens that block ultraviolet light; carbon nanotubes and graphene add strength and conductivity to composites; quantum dots are used as colour converters in some displays.
  • Electronics. Transistor gates are now a few nanometres long, and this is nanotechnology in mass production, not in a laboratory.
No nanobot hype

Most "nanotechnology" in the market is materials — particles, coatings, composites — not tiny machines. Medical nanorobots that repair the body from inside are research ideas, not products. A question that offers "nanobots that cure all diseases" as an option is offering a distractor. Also, nanoparticles are not automatically safe: their large surface area makes some of them more reactive and potentially more toxic than the bulk material, which is why regulation exists.

The instruments that made the field possible are the scanning tunnelling microscope (STM, 1981) and the atomic force microscope (AFM), which can image and even move individual atoms.

22.3 The Big Bang theory and Hubble's law

22.3.1 The evidence

The Big Bang theory says that the universe was once far hotter and denser than it is now, and that it has been expanding and cooling ever since. It is supported by three independent observations.

  1. The expansion. Distant galaxies recede from us, and the farther one is, the faster it recedes.
  2. The cosmic microwave background (CMB). A faint radiation fills all of space, with a nearly perfect blackbody spectrum at 2.725 K. It is the cooled remnant of the hot, opaque plasma that filled the universe until about 380 000 years after the beginning, when atoms formed and light could travel freely.
  3. The light elements. The observed abundances of hydrogen, helium-4 (about 25 % by mass), deuterium and lithium match the predictions of nuclear reactions in the first few minutes.

The CMB was found by accident by Penzias and Wilson in 1965 and mapped in detail by COBE, WMAP and Planck. Its tiny temperature ripples (about one part in 10^{5}) are the seeds from which galaxies grew.

22.3.2 Redshift

Light from a receding source is stretched to longer wavelengths. The redshift is

z=\frac{\lambda_{obs}-\lambda_{emit}}{\lambda_{emit}}

For small redshifts (small compared with 1) the recession speed is

v\approx cz

so z=0.01 means about 3000 km s⁻¹. For large redshifts this linear formula fails and the full relativistic relation is needed; the paper only uses the small-z form.

The cosmological redshift is not quite a Doppler shift through space: space itself is expanding while the light travels, so the wavelength is stretched all the way along the path. For exam purposes the difference does not matter, but the correct picture is "expansion of space", not "galaxies rushing through space".

22.3.3 Hubble's law

In 1929 Hubble found that the recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to its distance:

v=H_0d

where H_0 is the Hubble constant. Its measured value is about 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ (different methods give 67–73; the disagreement is the "Hubble tension"). One megaparsec is 3.09\times10^{22} m, or 3.26 million light years.

The law does not mean that we are at the centre. Every observer, in every galaxy, sees the same proportional recession: the expansion is uniform, like raisins moving apart in a rising loaf of bread. There is no centre and no edge.

22.3.4 The age of the universe

If the expansion had always had its present rate, a galaxy now at distance d would have been at our position a time d/v=1/H_0 ago. So 1/H_0 is a rough estimate of the age:

\frac{1}{H_0}=\frac{3.09\times10^{22}\ \text{m}}{70\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}} =4.4\times10^{17}\ \text{s}\approx14\ \text{Gyr}

The accepted age is 13.8 billion years, slightly less than 14 Gyr because the expansion was faster in the past (the galaxies were braking under their mutual gravity) and is speeding up now under dark energy. The estimate 1/H_0 is therefore an upper limit for a universe whose expansion is slowing, and a rough figure in any case. Quote it as "about 14 billion years", and quote the accepted value as 13.8.

Quantity Value (approximate)
Age of the universe 13.8 Gyr
Hubble constant H_0 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹
1/H_0 14 Gyr
CMB temperature 2.725 K
CMB last-scattering time 380 000 years after the Big Bang
Redshift of the CMB z\approx1100
Ordinary (baryonic) matter about 5 % of the energy budget
Dark matter about 27 %
Dark energy about 68 %
Three statements that are wrong
  1. "The Big Bang was an explosion in space." It was an expansion of space; there is no centre from which galaxies fly out.
  2. "The universe has an edge." The observable universe has a horizon, but the whole universe is not known to have an edge.
  3. "Hubble's law proves the galaxies are moving away through space." It describes the expansion of the space between them. On small scales — inside a galaxy or a cluster — gravity holds things together, and Hubble's law does not apply.
Worked example 22.2 — a galaxy's distance

Problem. A galaxy is observed with a redshift z=0.02. Taking H_0=70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, estimate its distance.

Solution. v\approx cz=3.0\times10^{5}\times0.02=6.0\times10^{3} km s⁻¹.

d=\dfrac{v}{H_0}=\dfrac{6000}{70}=86 Mpc.

Check. 86 Mpc is about 280 million light years. The redshift is small enough that the linear formula is acceptable (2 % error at this level).

Worked example 22.3 — the Hubble time

Problem. Show that 1/H_0 with H_0=70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ gives about 14 billion years.

Solution. Convert H_0 to SI: H_0=\dfrac{70\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}}{3.09\times10^{22}\ \text{m}} =2.27\times10^{-18}\ \text{s}^{-1}.

\dfrac{1}{H_0}=\dfrac{1}{2.27\times10^{-18}}=4.4\times10^{17} s =\dfrac{4.4\times10^{17}}{3.16\times10^{7}}=1.4\times10^{10} years.

Check. 14 billion years is the right order; the accepted 13.8 Gyr is close because the correction for the changing expansion rate is only a few per cent.

Formula and fact sheet

Item Fact or formula
Quarks u, d, c, s, t, b; charges +\frac{2}{3},-\frac{1}{3},+\frac{2}{3},-\frac{1}{3},+\frac{2}{3},-\frac{1}{3}
Leptons e, μ, τ (charge -1) and \nu_e,\nu_\mu,\nu_\tau (charge 0)
Proton, neutron uud (charge +1), udd (charge 0)
Pions \pi^+=u\bar d, \pi^-=\bar ud, \pi^0 a u\bar u/d\bar d mixture
Hadrons baryons =qqq; mesons =q\bar q; both feel the strong force
Baryon number +\frac{1}{3} per quark, -\frac{1}{3} per antiquark; conserved
Annihilation e^++e^-\to2\gamma, each 0.511 MeV
Pair production threshold 2m_ec^2=1.02 MeV, needs a nucleus nearby
Strong force gluon; range \sim10^{-15} m; strength 1
Electromagnetic photon; infinite range; strength \sim10^{-2}
Weak W^\pm, Z^0; range \sim10^{-18} m; strength \sim10^{-6}
Gravity graviton (hypothetical); infinite range; strength \sim10^{-38}
Higgs H^0, mass about 125 GeV/c^2, discovered at CERN 2012; gives mass to fundamental particles
Nanoscale 1–100 nm; 1\ \text{nm}=10^{-9} m
Redshift z=(\lambda_{obs}-\lambda_{emit})/\lambda_{emit}; v\approx cz for small z
Hubble's law v=H_0d; H_0\approx70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹; 1\ \text{Mpc}=3.09\times10^{22} m
Hubble time 1/H_0\approx4.4\times10^{17} s \approx14 Gyr
Age of universe 13.8 Gyr
CMB 2.725 K, emitted 380 000 years after the Big Bang, z\approx1100

Chapter summary

  • The Standard Model has six quarks and six leptons, in three generations, each with an antiparticle of the same mass and opposite charge.
  • Quarks are confined: only combinations are seen. Baryons are three quarks (p=uud, n=udd); mesons are a quark–antiquark pair (\pi^+=u\bar d).
  • The four interactions are strong (gluon), electromagnetic (photon), weak (W, Z) and gravitational (graviton, not yet observed), with strengths in the approximate ratio 1:10^{-2}:10^{-6}:10^{-38} and ranges from 10^{-18} m to infinity.
  • The Higgs boson (about 125 GeV/c^2, found at CERN in 2012) is the quantum of the field that gives mass to fundamental particles — not to the photon or gluon, and not most of the mass of a proton.
  • Nanotechnology works at 1–100 nm, where the surface-to-volume ratio is large and quantum effects set in; real uses include drug delivery, water treatment, coatings and nanoscale transistors.
  • The Big Bang is supported by the expansion, the 2.725 K CMB and the abundances of the light elements.
  • Redshift z=\Delta\lambda/\lambda, with v\approx cz for small z; Hubble's law v=H_0d with H_0\approx70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
  • 1/H_0\approx14 Gyr is a rough age; the accepted age is 13.8 Gyr, and the expansion has no centre.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — six: up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom, in three generations of two.

2. (b) — two up quarks and one down: +\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=+1, the proton charge.

3. (d) — up-type quarks (u, c, t) carry +\frac{2}{3}e; down-type (d, s, b) carry -\frac{1}{3}e.

4. (a) — the positron has the electron's mass and the opposite charge; it is the first antiparticle found (1932).

5. (c) — the muon is a heavy electron, a fundamental lepton. Protons and neutrons are baryons, the pion is a meson.

6. (b) — gluons bind quarks and hold the nucleons together; the photon carries the electromagnetic force.

7. (a) — the W and Z bosons are very heavy, which confines the weak force to about 10^{-18} m, far less than a nucleon.

8. (d) — ATLAS and CMS at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced the discovery in July 2012.

9. (b) — about 125 GeV/c^2, roughly 133 proton masses. 938 MeV is the proton and 511 keV the electron.

10. (c) — hadrons are the strongly interacting composite particles: baryons and mesons.

11. (a) — three quarks, as in the proton and neutron. A quark–antiquark pair is a meson.

12. (d) — a meson is a quark bound to an antiquark, which is why it has integer charge and baryon number zero.

13. (c) — u\bar d: +\frac{2}{3}-(-\frac{1}{3})=+1, the charge of \pi^+.

14. (b) — three quarks at +\frac{1}{3} each give B=+1; the antiproton has B=-1.

15. (a) — the strong force is roughly a hundred times the electromagnetic force at nuclear separations, hence the ratio 1:10^{-2}.

16. (d) — 1 to 100 nm: above a single atom (0.1 nm) and below a virus (about 100 nm).

17. (b) — a nanometre is 10^{-9} m, a millionth of a millimetre.

18. (c) — 2.725 K, the cooled remnant of the hot early universe; 300 K would be room temperature.

19. (a) — recession speed is proportional to distance, with H_0 as the constant of proportionality.

20. (d) — about 70 km s⁻¹ for every megaparsec of distance; the unit must have distance in the denominator.

21. (b) — 13.8 billion years from the Planck measurements; 4.6 billion is the age of the Earth.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — +\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=0. The quarks keep their charges; the total is zero, so the neutron is neutral.

2. (d) — energy 2m_ec^2=1.02 MeV shared by two photons, emitted back to back so that momentum also balances.

3. (a) — the strong force between quarks does not weaken with distance in the usual way; pulling them apart makes new quark pairs instead of freeing one.

4. (c) — the weak force changes quark flavour, turning a down quark into an up quark and emitting a W^-; the strong and electromagnetic forces cannot do this.

5. (b) — gravity is about 10^{-38} of the strong force; between two protons the electrical repulsion is some 36 powers of ten larger than their gravitational attraction.

6. (d) — the Higgs mechanism gives mass to the W and Z bosons, quarks and charged leptons. Photons and gluons stay massless, and most of a nucleon's mass comes from gluon-field energy.

7. (c) — at 10 nm a large fraction of the atoms sit on the surface, and quantum confinement changes the allowed energies, so colour, melting point and reactivity all shift.

8. (a) — the CMB is a nearly perfect 2.725 K blackbody coming from every direction, exactly what a hot, dense early universe cooled to about 3000 K and then released would leave behind.

9. (b) — v=H_0d is linear, so doubling d doubles v.

10. (d) — the wavelength is stretched by the expansion of space during the light's journey; it is not a Doppler shift through a static space.

11. (a) — the formula assumes a constant rate; the real expansion was faster in the past, so the true age (13.8 Gyr) is a little less than 14 Gyr.

12. (c) — the pion is a meson (quark–antiquark), with baryon number zero. The other three are three-quark states.

Answers and explanations — Set C
